utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Would you please call the case, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Witness. Did you have a good rest yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you watch the soccer game last night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only in part. I didn't have time to watch the whole thing unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. But however, we have to come back to your testimony. Well, Mr. Morrissey, are you ready for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am, but my learned friend has asked if he might put another document which by way of an oversight he didn't put and we agree with that being done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, I know I'd said I finished on Tuesday, but there was a document I neglected to put to him and with Your Honours' leave, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit D238.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have the document there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Right. It's a document of the 2nd of October, 1993, a security administration report to the Main Staff of the armed forces of the ABiH, signed by Jozo Jozic, the secretary for the SDB. I want to ask you about this document. It's a letter which -- report which has gone to the military security service. What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just take a minute to look at the document. You would need to go through the entire document to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours -- I'm sorry. I won't interrupt. Your Honours, perhaps it could assist the witness if it's made clear what he's being asked to comment upon. Obviously he can't be asked to comment on the truth or otherwise of the document because it's not suggested that he was there. But the Prosecutor is entitled to ask him to comment on the form of it and how it came to go from one agency to another, that would be legitimate, but it should be made clear to the witness what he's being asked, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, maybe you could put your question more specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, I'm not asking you to comment on the truth or otherwise of the document; that wasn't in my question. What I'm asking you about is as with the other documents, the form of the document and the manner how it was compiled and the type of document that it is.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say this about the document: It was a document produced by the state security service and in most cases here we've had documents drafted or produced or forwarded by the various public security services, the Ministry of the Interior, the police stations, and other such bodies. This is a state security document and it was signed on behalf of the deputy secretary Jozic, Jozo. It was signed by Nedzad Ugljanin. The document was produced by this service and as far as the signature is concerned, it is perfectly regular. The document reports about what happened in Grabovica. It hints briefly that there was a killing in that area and states that it was not possible for them to carry out an on-site investigation because the police station was not allowed to access the area. There is nothing more in this document about the problem, but as I've been explaining during this testimony the state security quite -- regardless of the work of the public security gathered information and informed the minister as well as both the military and the civilian authorities. This is a perfectly regular document, and it was produced by this body.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What is the status of a document of this type, that is a letter from the secretary -- under-secretary of the SDB to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document implies that this body had reliable information if they decided to go to one of the other institutions with this information. This document does indicate certain elements. For example, the field report from the state security service, and there's a reference here to a state security service report from Jablanica, which means this is something they received when reports were exchanged. It's a serious document, also in view of who it was addressed to. If I could just add this. In my previous testimony, situations were discussed in which the Ministry of the Interior might have been involved in some form of cooperation with the army, maybe to take over some tasks on behalf of the army. It was perhaps not entirely just that I only mention the name of General Jasarevic as the person who issued those requests. Any military bodies would have been entitled to issue these requests. We had security services centres throughout the country who got involved at the request of any corps, for example. So the understanding should not be that it could only have been pursuant to a request made by Jasarevic because even before Jasarevic there was an incumbent who also used to make requests and cooperation would follow just the same. So much for that particular explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. What's the status of this document? It's been admitted into the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's already admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think the Defence tendered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alispahic. Just on that point that you raised by way of explanation before. Mr. Jasarevic's predecessor was Fikret Muslimovic in the position of director of the SVB, military security service. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe there's no translation to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Let me ask it again and I'll see. You mentioned a moment ago that it may well be other persons than General Jasarevic who would made requests for measures to be taken. And I just wanted to ask you: Was General Jasarevic's predecessor at the military security service a man named Fikret Muslimovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And apart from those two persons, your service would respond to an appropriate request from other military bodies, even at the corps level. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But it also is the case - you can tell us if this is true - that where measures were to be taken against somebody of General Halilovic's seniority, the fact of such measures would necessarily be made known to the commander or the senior officer of the SVB. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just in order to explain, when you say the same level of seniority, I don't think there was anyone quite of the same level of seniority because there was only one Chief of Staff, at least as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I think we have a translation issue there because I didn't mean to say somebody of the same level of superior -- of seniority. What I meant to say was that somebody who was as senior as Sefer Halilovic, when measures were contemplated or indeed adopted against such a person, that fact had to be made known to the commander of the SVB or the director of the SVB. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to interpret your question and I ask the Chamber to understand what I'm trying to say. I can only give you my opinion and I can only talk about how it would have been in the Ministry of the Interior because the military bodies had their own system, organised in their own way. There was certain documents which they used in their work, and it was based on these documents that they took measures or decided measures should be taken. It was logical that all measures should be approved at a certain level, depending on the level on which these measures were being taken or applied and what precisely needed doing. So if I can please have the Chamber's understanding in this. I am a former minister, but I'm not trying to explain the inner workings of command and control because I simply do not believe I am qualified to be doing that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for that indication. At a later stage, I have to ask you some questions about that, but I understand your answers as well. Now, the next thing, Mr. Alispahic, that I wanted to deal with was a meeting of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 26th of November of 1993. And I'm going to show you a document which is a transcript of that meeting and ask for certain comments by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown this document. Your Honours, could I indicate --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Alispahic, I just indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: This document is not uploaded; it's only partially translated. We will provide a full translation as soon as is possible. We believe it to be a publicly accessible document, so we hope it's not too controversial in that regard. But we'll -- what I have in mind is to give Mr. Alispahic the chance to read parts of this or indeed all of it if he wishes, although some of it is quite lengthy, and to comment upon what is said there. Very well. And I ask that a Bosnian copy be provided, please, to Mr. Alispahic so that -- an English copy is being provided. Now, Your Honours, perhaps if that could be given an MFI number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, that's a fairly lengthy document that's been provided to you, and should you wish to read the entire thing, you should be given that opportunity. The parts I wish to take you to are quite confined because they concern Sefer Halilovic and what was said about Sefer Halilovic by the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, on that occasion. So that's going to be the focus of my questions, but of course you are entitled to see the whole document if you feel that it's necessary to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, this document will be MFI 435.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, perhaps before you start reading could I just ask you some general questions, please, about the Presidency. First of all, the Bosnian political -- the Bosnian constitution at the time provided for a Presidency, and in October and November of 1993 the president of the Presidency was Alija Izetbegovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Some of these questions may seem to be relatively basic questions, but I have to establish the basis for what I'm about to do. Secondly, I think you indicated the other day that you as Minister of the Interior sometimes attended meetings of the Presidency. And I want to ask you: Were you yourself, formally speaking, a member of the Presidency as -- by virtue of being Minister of the Interior at that time?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I see. Nevertheless, you attended at meetings when invited to do so because of your specific area of responsibility. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I was asked to attend meetings when problems that had to do with the Ministry of the Interior were being discussed. I had to be there in order to contribute to the Presidency's work because I was well-placed to help them along with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. And it's the fact that the Presidency had meetings from time to time, attended by members of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, Mr. Kljuc, Komsic, and other persons who were present, Mr. Silajdzic as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Silajdzic was not a member of the Presidency. It was Pejanovic, Mirko Pejanovic at that time, Tanja Lujic-Mijatovic, and I may leave someone out but I think it was those persons. Haris Silajdzic was prime minister at the time I think, and if he attended any meetings of the Presidency, there must have been specific reasons for him to be there, something to do with the government. A Ganic would be there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that. Now, do you recall whether you attended a meeting of the Presidency on the 26th of November, 1993, a transcript of which has been placed in front of you? I should indicate that I've observed no mention of your name speaking in there, but you may have a memory. So I ask you whether you can recall.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, there are some passages of this which I wish to take you to and perhaps I could ask you to look at page 22 of the Bosnian version. Now, I'm going to put a part of this to you and then ask for your comment about it. At page 22 -- just excuse me a moment. While that's being prepared for -- just excuse me a moment, please, Mr. Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a slightly unwieldy process, I appreciate, but it seems the most -- the quickest way to deal with the material hat we have in our possession. Could I indicate that the partial transcript, unfortunately, is not -- is taken from segments of the transcript where Alija Izetbegovic is speaking. But really for time reasons I think we haven't been able to translate every word of it, and there are some parts that come before -- even within Mr. Izetbegovic's speech, there are some parts that come before what is interpreted here, what is translated here. So having said that, of course any relevant part can always be put.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But I want to put this part to you. It seems that there was a discussion about the creation of ranks within the Bosnian army structure. Do you recall that topic being a matter of concern within the Bosnian army at about that time, namely the creation of ranks?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As concerns the organisation of the army and its inner workings, especially as the army was being organised, I really can't say much. Many things kept changing. There were different needs that would arise over time and all I know is that ranks were created and certain documents adopted, defining how this was to be done. But I don't think I'm sufficiently qualified to make any professional statements about this. I am saying what I'm saying simply because I was there at the time and I was to some extent involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I bear in mind your reservation, Mr. Alispahic, and I won't ask you professional questions on that basis. What I'm really asking you here is just as a matter of the chronology in this case, in about November 1993 you were aware, in general terms, that ranks were being created in some way within the army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the fact that they had started doing that; that was one of the tasks that had to be carried out to develop the army. It's necessary to have order, a hierarchy, et cetera, in all armies throughout the world. I think that's quite normal in an army and I didn't give it any more thought than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that. But from your -- the position that you had you also became aware, I take it, that Sefer Halilovic, even though he had been removed from the post of Chief of Staff, came to be given the rank of general. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Sefer Halilovic held the rank of general. As for the reasons and circumstances under which someone is conferred a rank, I don't know, nor do I know the circumstances under which Mr. Halilovic was conferred the rank of general. But I do know that he holds the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Now, this transcript that I'm now taking you to commences with a discussion about that topic. I won't ask you technical questions about it, but what I'm interested in is what the president said about mistakes made by Halilovic and the reasons why things were done in the way that they were. Now, the passage I ask you to read, and I'm going to read it out now as well so that we know each what we're talking about is a paragraph beginning with the words: "As for Sefer Halilovic, he is currently working at the Main Staff." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I just want to take you through this and then ask for some comments by you. "As for Sefer Halilovic" -- and this is from the section -- from some of Alija Izetbegovic's comments. "As for Sefer Halilovic, he is currently working at the Main Staff. His assignment is dependent on other matters and further consideration by the Ministry of National Defence or the Main Staff. I do not know what position he could take over. We wanted to show that no major mistakes have been identified. Mistakes have been made that make him unsuitable to stay on as the chief of the main staff but not such mistakes as mean he must be somehow sidelined from the army. On the contrary, he has performed great services. We must not now allow ourselves" -- sorry, pardon me. "We must not allow ourselves to neglect this fact. It is true that he has made certain mistakes and omissions but he deserves credit for being involved in the army's creation from the outset. It is two years now since they started out, so we think that the two of them are on an equal footing. "So he would have stayed at level one ... otherwise he would be general of a division, at the very least, if what had happened had not actually happened. However, this is a proposal that can be defended and opposed all day long. After a great deal of consideration, this seemed to be the right solution." Now, I just ask you to go now to page 27 and approximately three lines from the top of that page you'll see a sentence beginning: "People think it's the people from Sandzak who are somehow on the carpet." Do you see that sentence? I'm sorry, Mr. Alispahic, we'll assist. Are you able to see that passage?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am following you quite well. Just go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll read and you can read along or ahead if you wish. "People think" -- perhaps before we go ahead, would you mind just looking at the previous page and confirming if this is a passage of Alija Izetbegovic speaking. So perhaps check page 26 to make sure that what I'm putting to you is accurate about that and then we'll go on. "People think that it's the people from Sandzak who were somehow on the carpet. They should be dissuaded from this view, if possible. Of course, nobody should be amnestied for big things. As for Sefer, there were only things that were cast in his teeth. He was questioned. This state is based on law. It was found that there had been no crimes. If there had been any, criminal proceedings would have been initiated against him, end of story. He did have a telephone conversation with Celo, but this evidence was not relevant for the court. The situation's clear. However, that conversation was also quite vague. This is why, in my opinion, he could not hold the post of Chief of Staff and should've been removed. Because only a man who's absolutely certain, who never hesitates, can hold such a post. Nothing else was found about him. On the other hand, much credit goes for him -- goes to him for the organisation of the Army." And that's where I stop. Now, could I just ask you about that, Mr. Alispahic. What is recorded in the transcript there, does that accord with the views that you knew Alija Izetbegovic to hold at the time?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I agree with the views of the president. What he said is probably what he thought, and this is reflected in the minutes of the session held at the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And to move from the president to you, yourself. That was also your position. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never expressed such a position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. But did you hold discussions with president -- with the president in your capacity as Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to the president about numerous issues, especially about security issues, about certain problems, about the complex security situation in the town and sometimes in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course. And although you had many duties, one of your important duties was to provide exactly that sort of advice and information to the president, as minister. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did provide information. Most of the information was written down, was in written form. The president would receive the information. Some of the information was returned. Some of the information remained in the Presidency and was made use of there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And perhaps just dealing with one aspect of the Trebevic investigation, it's the fact that the Trebevic operation which took place on the 26th of October was a fully legal operation which went ahead with the approval of the president, Alija Izetbegovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this operation is concerned, the entire Presidency discussed it, not just the president of the Presidency. The entire Presidency took that decision. If someone wanted to speculate about the political validity of this decision, I don't think that that would be possible. The entire Presidency took that decision. And if my opinion counts for anything, I think that I also played an important role in that operation. I was directly involved in the operation and in carrying it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And because of -- sorry, perhaps I should make it clear, less there be any doubt. We are not seeking to cast any doubt on the validity of the operation at all. But I have some questions about the important tasks that you had to perform. Once the Trebevic operation had commenced and once the two commanders had been arrested and neutralised, one part of your function was to continue to brief the president as to the way in which the investigation was proceeding. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't my task. That was the task of the military service. You can check that. Both commanders were taken in. Ramiz Delalic and Caco were taken to the 1st Corps command. They were never in the Ministry of the Interior and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The question has created a problem. Perhaps I'll let the interpreter finish what he was interpreting but then I'll clarify that. I was really using that arrest as a time point. I'm not suggesting that you had any involvement in those and the evidence has already been given about it. Let me put it another way. From the 26th of October following that, in the days following, you did continue to liaise with the president and provide him with information that came to you concerning the Trebevic operation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now -- well, just excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I offer that transcript for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And could you brief me about the source of this document, the chain of the custody of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document, the Bosnian version of it has been disclosed to us by the Prosecution and as far as we can see represents a transcript of a presidential hearings that were heard on a regular basis. I think the Prosecution have disclosed a number of such transcripts over time, and not all of them are to be used in evidence here. But this is one disclosed to us. Mr. Izetbegovic is no longer alive, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And was the translation done by yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The translation is -- Your Honours, can I say that the translation, as it currently stands, is a hybrid translation. Some of it is done by CLSS, but I asked for a -- an additional part of the translation, which will be on the third page to be done. It's simply been done by a team member, so that the last page there is not an authorised translation. But it follows on where the official translation ended on page 27. And because there seemed to be a possible doubt as to the context of what was being said, I thought it appropriate to have that done. Now, I can ask the witness to read it into the transcript, but it seems that the most elegant solution would be that we offer this English transcript now and when a fully authorised transcript becomes available, we'll move to substitute that into evidence. And of course if it departs in any material way, well, then that might be something that could raise a controversy later, but we think it won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document is admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And the Court Deputy will assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D435.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, can I indicate I'm going to be changing topics now, and I wish to move now to some of the documents which the Prosecutor asked you to look at in the course of the evidence in-chief here. These chiefly concern operative information of various sorts which came into your hands in your capacity as minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown -- just excuse me. My cross-referencing document is gone. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 429, that was Prosecution document 169 -- sorry, 165.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The document that's coming up on your screen is dated the 28th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please enlarge that a little?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you have that document in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the learned Prosecutor asked you some questions about the form of this, and my questions will relate to the form and then there will be a couple of questions about the substance as well of it. In this case, who is the author of that document? Is this -- and perhaps I should make it clear, it might not be on your page. Is it Munir Alibabic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly did sign the document, but I believe that the police station, which was in the clinical in Kosevo, compiled a report on the incident and the chief of the police station, Alibabic, transformed this into a report and mentioned the individuals who are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is it possible to work out from the document who -- or what is the name of the person who provided the report to Munir Alibabic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if we could find the exact name, but we could certainly get the report from the police station, the document on the basis of which this was stated. And I say that the name of the person and the date of birth were mentioned. All the other particulars were included, the particulars that are usually noted down by the police. I believe that this is an authentic document and that what is alleged in the document is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can't ask you about whether the document is telling the truth or not. I should ask this - don't take this the wrong way - you didn't witness this incident yourself of course. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is certainly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. The difficulty for us in this court, Mr. Alispahic, is that we have this document to deal with. So I've asked you the question as to whether we can get the name of the person from the face of the document; you've answered that. Is it possible to infer from the document that it was written by someone connected with the police station at the hospital or at the clinic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I ask you to clarify what you mean when you say "connected."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I used the term "inferred," but -- well, perhaps I'll ask you this. In the normal course of events, you would expect that Munir Alibabic would base this report on what he was told by the police at the scene of the incident. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you're right. The police drafted a report on the incident, and it's on the basis of that report that Alibabic compiled this report, and this was done for two reasons, firstly because the police station is in contact with the security services centre and the security services centre can be in touch with the bodies referred to here to whom the report was forwarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So it's likely there's another report. Is that the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just one report. There were not two reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. And moving to the substance of this document, you observe here that there's reference on three occasions to the unit which was -- to which the wrong-doing soldiers belonged. Can I ask you to confirm that that unit is identified in the Bosnian version on each occasion as the 9th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this document only concerns one occasion, and the individuals involved are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I am having some questions -- some trouble with putting the questions properly here. On three occasions in the text the term "9th Mountain Brigade" is referred to. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. It is the fact that Ramiz Delalic's brigade was the 9th Motorised Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And we also have evidence here, but I'll ask you to confirm it, that within the organic structure of the 1st Corps there was a 9th Motorised Brigade and a 9th Mountain Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say because the names of the units changed. There was the motorised unit, then the mountain unit. On one occasion it was the motorised unit and then it was the mountain unit. So in fact I think you're wrong. I think that the unit in question is the same one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, let me just -- we can show you a diagram, if need be, drawn by General Karavelic in this court. But the evidence has been given by a variety of witnesses that there was two separate institutions, the 9th Motorised and the 9th Mountain. Now, I understand you were from the ministry rather than from the army. Could I ask you to cast your mind back and see if you remember whether there were two such units, in other words, the 9th Motorised and the 9th Mountain?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't confirm that. I have remembered the 9th Brigade. As to whether it's the 9th Motorised Brigade or the 9th Mountain Brigade, I don't know. But when I use these terms, I'm thinking of the same unit. I'm thinking of Ramiz Delalic's unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand you are thinking of that. Do you agree with me, though, that there's -- well, in any event, you -- could you just confirm for the Judges that there's no reference in the document that you've got there to the 9th Motorised Brigade. Just have a look over it and see if you can see in the Bosnian any reference to the 9th Motorised.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is what the document says. I don't think it's necessary for me to confirm that. It says the 9th Mountain Brigade. I don't know if it's necessary to read through the entire contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. It's not an attempt to be clever at your expense in any way, Mr. Alispahic. It's just that we've got the English version in front of us, and the Judges and I don't read Bosnian. So, anyway, we're just asking you to confirm that if you can. That's the end of the questions on that document. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I would now ask that the witness please be shown document -- Exhibit 430.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, what's being brought up on the screen before you is a document from the 6th of July, 1993 concerning intelligence about the 10th Mountain Brigade, and you were shown this document I think earlier in the week.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this document it's headed -- or it commences with the term "certain intelligence." Can you say, first of all, who is the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can check to see who signs the document. But as to who drafted it, there is probably a certain procedure that was followed to draft this document. I think that this is a sort of report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it's a great help to us for you to explain how these reports come about. As to the author or the person who signed it, on my Bosnian copy I simply can't make that out but you may be able to recognise it. Are you able to help with that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can have a minute to look through the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would you mind repeating your answer; the interpreter didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could please scroll the document down for me because I can't see the whole thing. All the way down, please. I think this document was signed by Jozo Jozic, who was then the chief of the state security service. The last time around, I noticed his signature was on one of these. You asked about how this document was produced. This is operative information that was produced based on operative intelligence collected from a number of different sources. Operative information must contain verified information because these reports are then forwarded to a number of different bodies. I think it had to be delivered to the military intelligence service and probably also to the Presidency or even the president himself. I was one of the users of this report; that much is certain. I think this is about a whole set of security-related information, about security-related matters. Based on that, this report was drafted to indicate how serious the security problem was. I think this is in reference to the 9th and 10th Brigades, Celo's unit, and Caco's unit. I think this is an overview of the security situation on the ground and it also speaks about the behaviour of some members of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. There's a passage -- a paragraph commencing with the words "we have" -- and this is at page 3 of the English, Your Honours. "We also have significant intelligence that on the 3rd of June, 1993, Sefer Halilovic held a meeting with Ramiz Delalic," and some details of such a meeting are then provided. Could I just ask you to find that passage and then I'm going to ask you some formal questions about it. I think it's the only reference to Halilovic in there. Could you just indicate when it is you've found that part. It may be that you'll find it on the last page of the document, three or four lines from the top.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can go ahead and ask the question. I haven't found the relevant portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, it's best if we find it for you. I'm sorry it's taking a little while. The section I'm talking about commences: "We also have significant intelligence that on the 3rd of June, 1993, Sefer Halilovic held a meeting with Ramiz Delalic and the command staff of the Delta Unit. On that occasion they advocated an attack against the Presidency of the republic and the capture of some Presidency members." It should be on the screen about three lines from the top.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the question I have for you is, if you know the answer to this, could you tell us who is the source of that information?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now, it's been 10 or 15 years. I can't say who the source was. I can only say who could have been the source or should have been the source. The media communications equipment and informants or perhaps measures taken by the military and state security services, measures imposed against a number of people who were of security interest, especially some who were in touch with Caco and Delalic. It was based on those contacts that this conclusion was arrived at probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. I thank you for that indication. Elsewhere in the document there is a reference to some other people, and I'm just going to ask you a couple of questions about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's said on page 4 of the English, Your Honours, "Some of the persons who were close to Musan Topalovic intended to leave Sarajevo, thus Mujo Zulic, commander of the 1st Mountain Brigade, attempted to leave the city with help of UNPROFOR, while Faruk Abadzic, unit commander in the 1st Mountain Brigade, Sakib Puskar and Ramiz Delalic had similar intentions." That section is towards the end of the document, you'll see, perhaps five or six lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I must ask you the same question about that information. Are you now able to tell us what the -- who the person was who gave that information, or is your answer essentially the same as to the previous question?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There might be some difference. We probably got this information from our contacts in UNPROFOR. It was very difficult to leave Sarajevo at the time. Those who wished to do so had to go to UNPROFOR for assistance. There was several ways to go about this. I noticed there were two legal ways to do it. If you were a government official, you had to file a request with UNPROFOR for a person to be taken outside of Sarajevo. Certain channels were used, the assumption was that there was a contact in UNPROFOR. You paid and you were allowed to leave Sarajevo. We're talking the security situation now, and this is the information that we obtained. My assessment is that there were a number of people around at the time who realised they could no longer be part of the command structure of the army. Some had already secured substantial financial gain for themselves and decided that they should leave Sarajevo. They no longer believed it necessary to stay in Sarajevo, since they would only be facing loss.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, thank you for that explanation, and those are the questions about that document. Now, could I ask that we move to another document. This is one that's not tendered in evidence yet. It's Prosecution Exhibit 65 ter number P150. And I'll just give you an MFI number. I think it's MFI 431 I believe, a document dated the 15th of June, 1993. Yes, it's 431. Now, this document that's coming up on the screen is one that you've seen before earlier this week and you were asked some questions about it by the Prosecutor. My questions to you really relate to the source, SS. Do you have that document in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. The assessment in paragraph -- sorry, paragraph 1 provides that: "In contact with the source SS, we obtained security-wise important information." Now, my question for you first of all is: Can you say -- before we get to SS, can you say who wrote this report or who drafted this official note?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the face of the document it appears that the official note was drafted by an operative of the state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Could you explain the formal reason why this report is not signed by a person who identifies themself, but rather is authored or drafted by a person with an operative number?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the procedure in the state security service. That's how it was done. If you look at the heading it says "operative member," then there is a code and the source is designated as SS. No name's given, as you see. This is a primary document of the state security service, and if I were in charge of deciding I would not release this document for further use myself. All information contained in a document like this is subject to verification. So that was what needed to be done. All the information had to be verified and that's all I could say about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm grateful for your indication and the questions have nearly finished about it. I just have to ask you about the source SS. Are you personally able to say who the source SS was?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anyone could tell you. You would need to get into the system. You would need to do a search and then maybe you would be able to track someone down or to find a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that indication. Those are the questions about that document there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since you finished this document, could we have a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break for 30 minutes and then we'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey, please continue your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you again, Mr. Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, could the witness now please be shown another document, Exhibit P207.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, the document that's coming up now is dated the 19th of September and it's the police report concerning an incident involving Ramiz Delalic, Celo, and or near to Pazaric at Hadzici. Do you have that document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in this case the proceedings or the pre-criminal proceedings and indeed the proceedings themselves concerning Ramiz Delalic were conducted by the military security service of the army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the military security service?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, the SVB.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were in charge. He was an officer of the army, and the military security service would take steps with regard to army members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And so cooperating with that investigation, this report was brought into being by the civilian police, effectively, to assist. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't quite say that. First of all, this document stemmed from the fact that the incident in Zovik near Pazaric was committed by Ramiz Delalic, Celo, who attacked a patrol of the military police. There was a fight that ensued and some people were injured. There was one police officer in particular. I remember that I was informed immediately by the local police station. I think there was this report that the military security -- state security service I think sent to the security administration, who probably conducted their own investigation. So this is no participation by the police in the investigation of Ramiz Delalic, Celo. This is an incident that occurred and all the perpetrators were known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes -- could I just ask -- this, the document we have here, seems to indicate that what is being alleged against Ramiz Delalic is an attack on members of the police station. The transcript here recorded you here as saying the military police, and I just-- I think I have to clarify that with you. Who were the victims in this case according to your information, military police or civilian police?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in this case, at least as far as I can tell based on the document, the civilian police, unless some members of the military police were there because sometimes there were mixed checkpoints that were manned together by the military and civilian police. The reason was it was easier to deal with incidents in this way. If an incident occurred that was caused by a military officer, then the military could take over and vice versa. This is a way that we found of dealing with these problems, and I can't speak about each and every name. I can't tell you whether they were military or civilian police officers. They may have been together, but I'm quite certain that a police representative was around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And as to the source of the information in this document here, although the -- the signature is somewhat obscured, are you able to comment whether that document is signed by Jozo Jozic? I think it's to be found on the second page of the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Jozo Jozic is the person who signed it. At the time he was chief of the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And are you able to say who provided this information to Jozo Jozic and in what form was it provided?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information could have been obtained from the Sarajevo state security sector. The state security service, in turn, could possibly have obtained a report from the Ducin [phoen] police station. That's where it was during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. And is it possible to identify on the face of the document who -- which individual people provided the information that you've just indicated?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if you consider the procedure used by the ministry, it should be possible to track the document down. The original should be somewhere in Tarcin kept by the police administration there. It has been a long time but there should be some sort of a paper trail that you can follow. There is a document to this effect. I know this for a fact because I was informed about this incident at the time in my capacity as minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can you recall who that document you got was composed by [sic]?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I read this document at the time. There was daily communication going on between the chief of the state security and the chief of the Ministry of the Interior. As to who compiled this document, now that's something that I really can't speak about. If I may, I believe this information is actually accurate, if you take into account the names given here. Those people really were around at the time. And there was this one police member who was hospitalised and I think there should be a document to that effect, to show that this member was hospitalised on account of severe injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can't ask you about the accuracy of the document, Mr. Alispahic, but I'm grateful to you for what you've said about the form of it. And now I would seek to move to another document which is Exhibit 238, a document of Jozo Jozic which is dated the 2nd of October, 1993. And here -- this is the document that the learned Prosecutor showed you this morning. Do you have that in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, again these are questions of form and questions about the sources, not questions about the truth or accuracy of the document. Firstly, are you able to say what sources Jozo Jozic relied upon to compile this short letter? Or short report, I should say.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a report was used that was obtained from the state security service stationed somewhere on the ground. They in turn probably had their own contacts in the area, including the Jablanica police station. They were probably in touch with them; they would have had to be to send a report like this to me. I believe it is a brief report but fairly accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I hear your answer there. I just want to put one specific part of it to you and ask you a very similar question. The section that says this: "Members of the military police of the RBiH army and the Jablanica SJB were unable to conduct an on-site investigation because there were indications that they, too, could be liquidated." Now, what was the source for that piece of information, if you're able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it could only have been the police station. There was daily communication between them at the time, especially in the area. They probably obtained this from the chief or the commander, someone like that, saying that it was impossible to carry out an on-site investigation, telling them what the situation was like because that was the sort of danger that they were talking about. Because the service sometimes manipulates certain things and they say there is every indication that this or that happened, so they're talking about a security problem. And they had in the area a state security detachment. They said they had tried to go to the area but were not granted access, wherein as members of the state security would not have been in charge. They didn't necessarily need to go there, but they were obviously able to provide a report like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And I think just to pick up what you said there, you personally made it very clear when you were in Jablanica and you spoke to Emin Zebic, you made it clear that the police in Jablanica should hold themselves out as ready to help whenever they were asked to by the army in relation to the Grabovica matter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In other words, it was an SVB investigation, but your organisation was of course prepared to help. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, insofar as it concerns our readiness. I can't tell you what the SVB did, whether they did anything at the time, whether they did anything about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. You can't tell me and I won't ask about that if you can't say. But I do want to move on to the next document and that's an information dated the 11th of the 10th, 1993. Just excuse me and I'll give you the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What is the 11th of 10th, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, the 11th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I apologise. Just excuse me while I match the exhibit number to the document. Just excuse me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. This will have an MFI number I think. This is MFI 434.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this document which is under the hand of Enver Mujezinovic, what sources -- are you able to say what the particular sources were upon which the author, Mr. Mujezinovic, relied in compiling this information?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say who the sources were. It was produced by the Sarajevo state security sector, specifically Enver Mujezinovic. It talks about indicative efforts. What that means is that it's there and yet it's not there. This information talks about something that needs to be taken into account or checked. There is every indication; this is the phrase used by the police. Information could be accurate or merely an evaluation, and that's why there is talk here of indication. There is nothing that is certain or reliable or there may not be anything there that is certain or reliable but could merely be used as an indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that explanation. Could we move, please, to Exhibit 415 now. Now, this document is undated, but it's possible to draw a conclusion about it that it was composed later than the 17th of October, 1993, because the content refers to incidents on the 17th of October, 1993. Do you have in front of you that document?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. This document contains a list of various informations concerning Ramiz Delalic, and in the first line of the substantive text it provides: "Through operative work in the field and taking other measures and actions in the domain of the service, among other things, we obtained much data pertaining to the abuse of the office overstepping the official authority and criminal acts committed by the 9th Motorised Brigade deputy commander, Ramiz Delalic." Now, are you personally able to say what the sources of the information in this document are? Of course we have the phrases in those two sentences. Are you able to add to that information that it's operative work in the field, other measures and actions in the domain of the service?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say anything about sources now, because it's impossible to determine the sources on the basis of documents. You can do this if you use the appropriate technology that various services have recourse to. If you had a look at the documents that served as a basis for this information, then you would be able to determine what the sources were. You have a summary of information for a given period in time that is of interest for security reasons. There are a number of issues here that refer to that officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown now P212, which I think is the last of the operative-information-sort-of documents that were shown to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, this one is another document that you were shown and it has the gloomy heading "report on the negative conduct and activities of Sefer Halilovic, Chief of Staff of the supreme command of the Army, Bosnia and Herzegovina Armed Forces." Now, this document -- could I just ask you some -- I'm not asking about the truth or otherwise of the allegations in there, but what I'm asking about is the form of the document and its sources. First of all, is it possible to say who -- from the document who it was who compiled this document or who drafted this document, I should say?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorities behind this document, the military security service and the state security service, those two services are concerned. This is a report on negative behaviour and work, and I think it was drafted after discussion with the general. Perhaps one could see or have a look at the date of the document. I believe that two copies were made. I believe that it was a state secret. The terminology used is military -- or rather, it says that the military service and the civilian authorities participated in drafting the document. Numerous documents were used, sources, information, data, information obtained for the report was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. As to the individual person who drafted it, are you able to say who that was?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. I really couldn't provide you with the name of the individual who drafted the report. It was probably -- or there were probably at least two individuals involved in drafting the document, since the document concerns two institutions. So the SDB and the military security service cooperated in drafting this report. As you have noticed, the title of the document is quite negative. It refers to the negative conduct of an individual, and these are terms often used in the military. But since it is a joint document, this doesn't seem a significant problem to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And whilst you're unable to identify the particular individuals who drafted this, are you able to comment on whether or not anyone senior from your organisation was one of the authors? And I have in mind those people whose signatures are on other documents, Jozo Jozic, or Enver Mujezinovic. And perhaps I'll try to phrase the question precisely. Is it likely or possible, given the form of this document, that either of those senior people is the author or -- is the author or part author of this document?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually reports are compiled by departments responsible for analysing things. They have all the information that relates to certain security issues, given the tasks they have to perform. When such a report is requested, when it's necessary to draft such a report, whatever the reason, these services propose a certain report on the basis of the information they have, on the basis of the documents they have. As for the final version of the documents concerned, the SDB chief, the state security service chief, or the supreme command staff would have to check the final version. I don't know whether it was the security service in the army or the army commander who would do that, but in the Ministry of the Interior the SDB chief is the last person to check all the reports from within the SDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And is there any indication on the face of this document that that was done on this particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your question; put it a little more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. You know the form of these documents well and we in this court are only grappling with the form. So I ask you whether you can assist. Is there anything on the face of this document which indicates whether it was finally checked by any person at the senior level, whether that be Mr. Jozic, Mr. Mujezinovic, or any other official at a senior level? For example, are there any initials or signatures or stamps or anything of that nature to indicate such a viewing?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we have a look at the document, then it's quite clear. There's a footnote here, perhaps there are several footnotes, which indicate that the report was drafted on the basis of certain documents. The author of this report had documents that were used to draft this report. As I have already said, the report was drafted at the two levels I have referred to. In the military service and the SDB there should be certain documents that were used to draft this report. Here it says that certain information has been obtained; that quite clearly indicates -- well, what does this mean? All you have to do is refer to the documents concerned, are these statements that have been made, or documents that refer to secret methods used by the SDB or is it something else. There might be certain confidential sources, people who cooperate with the military and state services. So if someone had a look at the report and read through it, well, one couldn't really discuss the weight one should attach to it, its authenticity, referring to it in professional terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes -- sorry, go on.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. There's something I would like to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the footnote it says that the document's reliable and to a certain extent there are court documents. There were documents that had been prepared for the needs of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, well we see that footnote and thank you for that explanation. That completes the questioning on that -- on those documents which you were shown by the Prosecutor, and thank you for your patience in dealing with them. Could I now move on to another topic. I now have some questions concerning chronology of the events at Grabovica and your movements at that time and how you came to know about the events. That's the focus of the next line of questioning that's coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown P118, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And this, Mr. Alispahic, is a document you were shown already. It's a document entitled "order to the 4th Corps command at Mostar," asking the 4th Corps command personally to inform Minister of Internal Affairs, Bakir Alispahic, to head for Jablanica tonight because he has a meeting tomorrow, 10 September, 1993, at 1900 hours in Konjic with Mr. Rusmir Mahmutcehajic. Now, to the best of your knowledge you indeed did what was suggested in this order, even though I understand you didn't receive the order personally. You did come back to Jablanica and ultimately on to Konjic and have a meeting with Rusmir Mahmutcehajic on the 10th of September, 1993, at approximately 1900 hours in Konjic. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. So now using that date, I'd just like to get a sense of the chronology of what you did before that and after that. Firstly, when you came to Konjic -- when you came back from Mostar to Jablanica, I want to ask you about your approximate departure time and how long it took you to get back there. Did you leave Mostar during the afternoon or in the evening of the 9th of September, the day before your meeting with Mahmutcehajic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think that this order arrived, as they wanted to inform me through the command; there was no other way this could have been done, through the police, but it was done through the army. Since Mahmutcehajic probably found it easier to do this through the army since he was in a military facility. So it was easy to send this document in this way. In Mostar I was informed that upon returning I was to have this meeting with Mahmutcehajic. And that concerns the reasons for this letter. And secondly, when I arrived in Jablanica I was in the Jablanica police station with Cemin [phoen], the chief, was present. I said that we had a meeting and other issues that were the responsibility of the MUP was concerned. And at the meeting I was informed about the events in Grabovica by the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could you provide -- sorry, I cut you off there. But could you provide an approximate time when you arrived in Grabovica that morning on the 10th -- I'm sorry, I take that back. I put in the fatal word "Grabovica." Let me take that back and start again. Could you give an approximate time when you arrived in Jablanica on the morning of the 10th?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't give you a precise time, since so much time has passed since then. It would be easier for me to focus on the event concerned, on the conduct concerned, rather than to focus on the precise time. Even in peacetime it was difficult to provide an indication of the precise time that something happened. All I know that the trip to Mostar and from Mostar -- well, we had to go on this trip in the evening because of the combat. So those are the circumstances that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Putting the matter as generally as possible then, did you arrive in Jablanica in the morning or in the afternoon of the 10th of September, to the best of your recollection at this date?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the morning. That day we were supposed to have a meeting in Konjic in the afternoon. In the morning, as I have already said, I was in the police station, or rather in the army command. And therefore, I think that I arrived in Jablanica in the morning and got involved in those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Now, working backwards from there you left Mostar at some stage in the evening on the previous day, the 9th of September. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I left Mostar the previous day and set off in the direction of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could I ask you this: It was necessary to travel overnight to get to Jablanica from Mostar because of the danger of fire from HVO positions at some points. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was necessary to travel at night because of one part of the road. You had to see when you would travel down the road that could be travelled down during the day. There was a more dangerous part of the road because of the fighting, and it would be safer to travel down that part of the road at night, although some people did so in the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And can you say approximately how long the journey took you to get from Mostar to Jablanica? And again, I understand you can't be minute-perfect or perhaps even hour-perfect. But just doing the best you can, what was the duration of that trip?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is how I would put it. As far as I can remember, when travelling to Mostar, given that many men carried weapons and had equipment, you needed far more time to get there. When you have a large column of men, you need a lot of time to get there. And I believe that it took us between 14 and 16 hours to reach Mostar. And when setting off from Mostar, there were few of us who were returning, myself, my security officers, and some civilians, and it took us far less time. The CSB from Mostar also assisted us, and they managed to escort us in military vehicles for a certain part of the route. I don't know how much time it took us, but it was significantly quicker because you had only a few people. The military has the statistics on how long it takes a soldier to travel a certain route if he is fully equipped, and I think this is something that has to be taken into consideration when estimating the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Anyway, the return back from Mostar to Jablanica was quicker than the trip from Jablanica down to Mostar with the Laste Unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And -- now, just to fix, if we can, the date which you went down to Mostar with the Laste Unit. Is that the fact that you set off from Jablanica to Mostar on the 8th of September and travelled overnight on the night between the 8th and 9th of September, arriving in Mostar on the morning of the 9th of September. Is that accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps what you said about going to Mostar is not quite correct. Perhaps you could obtain the document that shows exactly when we set off for Mostar, when the Laste Special Unit set off at the time I was with them, and that would help you to determine when I left for Mostar, when I was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, we have to work with -- in this court we have to deal with live evidence, and I really have to put the questions to you about this. But perhaps you -- perhaps we can work it out. Do you recall how long you personally were in Mostar on this particular occasion? Were you there for a full day or less or more?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember exactly how much time I spent in Mostar. All I can say is that from the 5th onwards the special unit went into the field. I think it's easy to find that document, but it's possible that I was in Mostar the day before because I had a meeting in the security services centre and in the 4th Corps command. But in the statement it says that when I arrived in the police station I was involved in the activities I was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And -- well, the Prosecution have provided that statement to us, of course, and I just wanted to ask you, if you can remember now, to clarify that, if possible. Can you recall what activities you did participate in in Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember that I was in the security services centre in Mostar, I had a meeting there with the company commander, Pasalic. I remember that the media was present. As far as I can remember, Beara was present. I had an interview on radio Mostar. I'm not sure what the name of the radio station was, and that is all I can remember. As far as the activities I was involved in during that period of time in Mostar are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You don't have a recollection of sleeping over at any hotel or any facilities overnight in Mostar on that occasion. Is that correct or wrong?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said it's possible that I spent two days in Mostar. Perhaps I was there on the 8th and the 9th, so naturally I had to sleep somewhere in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Well, thank you. Well, I appreciate your efforts to recall these things, too, and we know it's 12 years ago, but you just have to do your best with this. Mr. Alispahic, very well. At a later time I'm going to come back to that because we have evidence from other witnesses that we have to compare your evidence to, of course. So I'm going to come back to that issue and give you a chance to comment on what some other people say. But for now I just want to move forward now. It's safe to say that you were in Mostar on the 9th, you came back to Jablanica and ultimately Konjic on the 10th. And are you able to comment what time it was that you had the meeting with Rusmir Mahmutcehajic. In the order on the screen it says it was scheduled for 1900 hours in Konjic. Can you recall if that was the approximate time of the meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say whether it was at 1900 hours or not, whether it was before or after. I know we had a meeting. I know where we met. I know what we talked about, and that's all I can say before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, I'm not going to ask you any questions about the substance of that meeting. You've given your account of that. But I'm still asking questions about the chronology. And you slept in the facility called the Ark that night, is that correct, that's the night of the 10th?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but I don't remember that I spent the night there. I think I had set off for Sarajevo, since it was nighttime and you had to travel by night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Are you able to say what the approximate duration of the journey from Konjic into Sarajevo was on this occasion? Again, doing the best you can to give an estimate.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't commit myself on the duration of the journey. I could give you an estimate on what I would expect the journey to take, but it all depends on the circumstances of travel. Getting into Sarajevo implied a late arrival, a nighttime arrival. The drive between Konjic and Tarcin could take about an hour, and the rest could take several hours. Usually it took the whole night to cross from one of these places to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Thank you. Now, did you get back to Sarajevo in the early hours of the morning of the 11th of September?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 11th of September, but I can't say when. Whether it was just past midnight or in the morning hours, really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember my position at the time, I was able to use a vehicle for this part of the journey but you had to keep the headlights off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recall whether or not you had a rest or a sleep before you came to your office and spoke to Commander Delic and then subsequently the president, Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I rested briefly, not much though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can you recall the approximate time at which you -- I'm sorry, Mr. Alispahic, you were still speaking. You speak quite softly and I started to speak over the top of you, but I cut you off. So could you finish what you were saying, please.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That time during those operations and all the things that were going on, we were all extremely exhausted and had little time to rest. Therefore, it was perfectly normal for one to get some rest, especially after nighttime arrivals in town, so that the next morning you could go about your duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could you give an approximate time, again doing the best you can, for when you made contact with Commander Delic on the morning of the 11th?
