utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it wasn't really in the morning. It could have been in the early afternoon [as interpreted], 10.00, as far as I can remember. What I remember is a visit to the Presidency because the President would normally be at work at about 10.00 or 11.00, so it was not in the early morning. It was around about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, you'd better guide us as to this. The timing of these meetings can be of some significance, Mr. Alispahic. So just doing the best you can, do you say the range of times within which you met Mr. Delic and Mr. Izetbegovic is between 10.00 in the morning and perhaps 2.00 in the afternoon? Would that be an accurate range to put?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think both meetings were over by noon. I'd say it was earlier, between 9.00 and 11.00, or between 9.00 and 12.00, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I thank you for that range. Very well. And can you recall in relation to those meetings the approximate timing of the telephone conversation that you indicated you had with General Jasarevic? Firstly, was it between those two meetings or was it after both of them had finished?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was after, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember a specific time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. All right. Now, I just have another question about travel distances. Again doing the best you can here, are you able to recall in those days how long it would take you to get from the supreme command headquarters in Sarajevo to Zenica, to the town of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. Sometimes it took longer; sometimes it didn't take that long. It depended on whether the roads were negotiable. It depended on which road you decided to take. There were different travel options, and it varied. It's next to impossible for me to give an estimate. There were some wartime situations. Sometimes it took as many as 24 hours to get to Zenica. I'm not tying myself down to a specific date; I'm just trying to give you a general idea of what it meant to go to Zenica at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. We're grateful for that indication and that's -- that assists. What's the -- I was going to ask you: What's the wartime speed record to get from Sarajevo to Zenica? In other words, what would be a good fast trip from Sarajevo to Zenica in about September 1993, if everything went well and cars didn't break down and all conditions were favourable?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer the question. I was hardly in a position myself to make the journey in one go. I never measured the time it took. I never did it in one go. I always had someone I was in touch with at Tarcin, Visoko, Fojnica, maybe people who were members of the army travelled between Sarajevo and Zenica which was in the nature of their work. So maybe they should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, indeed, of course we have some evidence from other witnesses about this question, but you are assisting by your answers and I just would persist a little bit further. If you were setting out from the Sarajevo headquarters of the supreme command, how long would it take you to get out through the tunnel -- perhaps I should ask you a preliminary question before that one. Was it necessary to go through the tunnel under cover of darkness in all cases?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could say yes and I could say no. Sometimes on account of my job I had to go in broad daylight, and the journey was a difficult one. Most people went under cover of darkness because it was safer. Secondly, sometimes the tunnel was closed for whatever reason, and you could only go one way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could assist with one other timing issue. What -- when you came out of the tunnel, what was that area called? We've had it referred to as Hrasnica. What was the name of the precise place that you found yourself in, having left Sarajevo and coming out of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Butmir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What was the timing -- to get from Butmir to Visoko, approximately how long would that journey take?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, we would need to distinguish between the various routes. There were several depending on the combat operations that were underway. There were roundabout routes, and sometimes it took 24 hours to reach Zenica. Zenica and Visoko were not isolated, not encircled, and sometimes you could get there in one or one and a half hours. There was several different ways to get to Visoko, several roads you could take. It's just very difficult for me to say, despite my best efforts to assist you in this and make an assessment. I simply don't believe that in those difficult days you could possibly have made the journey in anything under eight to ten hours, but that's just an assessment on my part. I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And the final question on these matters concerns one more leg of a potential journey. Leaving aside any delays caused by shelling or other accidents, how long would it take to get from the headquarters of the army in Sarajevo to Butmir? In other words, to get to the airport and to go through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the journey was smooth in a manner of speaking, then in my estimate it would take about one or one and a half hours to reach the end of the tunnel from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much for those timing questions. Just excuse me, I'm just going to move to another topic. Very well. Thank you very much. Now, I want to turn to some questions concerning some transcripts of telephone conversations that have been provided to the Defence in this case. And I've got some questions about those. That will probably take us out for the rest of the day I would think, those questions. Now, first of all, the learned Prosecutor asked you questions yesterday -- I'm sorry, on Tuesday, concerning the application of the wire-tapping or telephone tapping method to Sefer Halilovic in 1993. So I have to follow up those questions with some specific other questions, and we'll proceed slowly through those. Now, first of all, you have indicated that although it was pursuant to an army request or, more specifically, an SVB request, your service cooperated by undertaking the operative measures of telephone tapping against Sefer Halilovic. Did those measures commence on the 10th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about the exact time. The measures commenced -- if you go back to the documents, it should be there. I don't think I could possibly answer the question since I was not in charge of the implementation. I didn't know about it. I just can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, let me -- I'll just have to deal with the structure of how this is done in general first and then perhaps come back to some questions about it. In general terms, when the method of phone tapping is applied to a person, there is some quite strict legal requirements about how such a measure is approved. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There certainly are a number of legal requirements; I agree with that. There are legal requirements defining these steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, in answer to some questions by the learned Prosecutor, you indicated that Sefer Halilovic had been the subject of some previous measures in the time before you became the minister. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said the same measures and not some previous measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So I think that's what I said, too, but perhaps we missed each other. In any event, when you became minister you found yourself in the position of making sure that from that time onwards things were done properly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And this is not the time to be discussing what happened previously, but you yourself had sufficient concerns about -- look, I simply won't ask you the questions about that previous time; you weren't the minister. Very well. Anyway, just going back to the procedures that have to be followed to put in place a -- the measure of telephone interception. Is it the fact that the sector chief or a senior official of the SDB, in order to get a telephone intercept approved, must submit a proposal to the minister and detail in that proposal a brief summary of the reasons why they need this measure to be put in place?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the procedure says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And is it also a requirement that then the minister is obliged to -- to assess this proposal and to issue a decision, either approving or not approving the implementation of these measures?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one of the reasons that these measures had to go to the minister for approval. Sometimes you had to go even higher up to get approval, the government or the Presidency, for example. I am talking about the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. No, I understand that you're confining it to the state security sector. And what are the sort of situations where you would need -- where the minister would need to go to the President in order to get approval for the implementation of a measure -- of this measure?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was necessary to obtain approval at that sort of level when measures were being applied to members of the government or high-ranking state officials. Everything else would have under the competence of the state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, apart from going to the Presidency, in the case of implementing a measure of this nature against a very senior army official, obviously we have in mind the case -- the concrete case of General Halilovic here, but I am speaking as a matter of general principle, too, apart from going to the Presidency, when dealing with a senior army person who was to be subject to these measures, was it necessary in those circumstances to advise the commander of the army? And secondly, was it necessary to advise the director of the military security service, the SVB?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure future SVB person is a director; I think in the military it's actually called chief. As for the question when measures are taken or imposed against members of the army regardless of their rank, this is governed by internal army regulations. The army had its own system in place defining the steps to be taken in these situations and how these measures were to be applied. Sometimes one needed to get approval for these measures to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I understand that. But -- well, perhaps could I move to a more specific situation. When the army -- when the commander of the army would seek the assistance of your organisation to help with the particular method of phone tapping in the course of one of their own investigations or their own inquiries, did they have to submit a written request to your organisation in order to get that assistance that they needed?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, there should be a document upon the basis of which the SDB would provide that sort of service. There must be a document showing the name of the person in question. These are the elements that you must bear in mind in order to impose these measures as well as the phone number and other such details. The document would take a certain form and would then be submitted to the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would you be able to explain to us what the form of -- what form that document would take? Would it be in the form of a letter, specifying why the army wanted the assistance of your service? Or was there a pro forma type of document to be used?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I really can't tell you whether it was a pre-typed form or not. There must be some that were used by the MUP or by the state security -- or rather, when these measures were being applied against someone from the MUP or state security, but when imposed against a civilian I really can't say what sort of form was used. I know that the chief of the SDB told me that these measures were being applied to a number of different individuals. But this was confidential, even in relation to other members of the SDB with the exception of the person who was implementing the measure, and then they would forward everything to -- including the documents, to the military security service. If there was anything of relevance, the military security service would write up their own report, a document, and would then pass it on to the SDB or the MUP whenever necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. And of course the role of the minister , in particular, the minister who was in your ministry, whether it was you or your predecessor or the person who came after you, the role of the minister did not include going and listening to telephone taps yourself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister doesn't listen to those telephone taps. Perhaps in exceptional circumstances I would hear certain conversations or listen to if serious issues were at stake. For example, an individual was at risk, facility was at risk, someone wanted to harm someone else, but I really do not remember ever having listened to such telephone intercepts, apart from when I was a young operations officer involved in such activities in the service. Civil servants don't listen to such intercepts; they receive transcripts, they receive the relevant documents that have already been processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Well, yes, thank you for that information. And now I just want to turn to some questions concerning what actually happens when a phone -- sorry, well, I'm changing topics now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So perhaps it might be a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break for 30 minutes and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey, please continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Alispahic. I was just going to move to the method that was used back in those days by the SDB when actual phone-tapping was occurring. I'll just put some propositions to you, you tell me if these are accurate or not. Once the minister had granted approval for a particular phone-tapping to take place, is it the fact then that individual employees to the service would listen to all telephone calls made from a particular telephone of the target?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you perhaps clarify the question. What do you mean when you say "all telephone calls"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Well, I understand. I'll address the question in slightly a different way. Once a person's telephone was approved -- I'll start the question again. Once the operative measure of telephone-tapping was approved against a particular individual, a team of employees was given the job of listening to that telephone, such team rotating in 24-hour shifts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And just looking at it from the working class's point of view for a moment, an individual SDB employee would work a 24-hour shift, and then he or she would hand over to another employee and they would work a 24-hour shift, and there was a team of three people in the normal course of events doing that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's correct, at least not in our service. There were no officials who would work a 24-hour shift as far as I can remember. They worked at a certain site, that's what we called it, or there were three officials working at one site. And they rotated in order to cover a 24-hour period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And just to clarify one term there, you used the word "site." We don't need to know physically where that was, but there was a particular location where the employee was allowed to listen to the target telephone, and that's what we call a site. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's like the place where I am now sitting and responding to your questions; that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, thank you. Now, it's typical of that sort of work that the worker -- I'm sorry. Perhaps could I just ask you this: What's the appropriate technical term by which we should refer to this worker who was doing the listening?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the term is now, but I think that they were called operators. I think that is how one called such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's what we'll call them. Now, with respect to the operators in a particular case, it's not necessary to mention any of their names in court now, but it is clearly possible to identify who was listening on a particular day by reference to the transcript that they may produce at a later time, is that correct, because they'll have a number?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it should be possible to determine the names of the individuals who were involved in those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. Well, we don't need to mention any names now here. But --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak up a little for the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The interpreter --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as far as that issue is concerned, well, I couldn't provide you with the names because I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. And the interpreter has just asked, Mr. Alispahic, if you would try to speak a little bit louder because they're having trouble hearing. Now, the process, I take it was this: That an operator would listen to the telephone and if they heard a telephone call that was of potential significance, then they should approach their supervisor or the person coordinating their activities and advise them that there may have just been an important telephone call. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is correct. If the conversation was alarming, if it was necessary to take certain other measures. But in principle this is not correct. In principle the operator compiles a report on the intelligence gained by intercepting telephone conversations. That is the technology that was employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. In the archives of the -- of the organisation known as FOSS -- well, look, I won't give evidence from the bar table. Can I just ask you this: Records of those telephone conversations were preserved in a verbatim handwritten form. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been typed out as well. It depended on the -- the equipment available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In terms of the compiling of those records, let's just stick with the handwritten record of the conversations, and I'm going to show you some examples of these in a minute but I just want the general principle now. But in terms of those handwritten ones, was the operator required to do a handwritten verbatim record of every single conversation, or was he or she just required to do a handwritten record of the ones which seemed to be of interest?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the operator would try to assess the intercepts that were important. These were seasoned operators and they realised what they had to record and what they did not have to record. And since there were audiotapes of the intercepts which were kept in the archives, it was possible to check these tapes if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. When the -- when the operator did the handwritten transcript of a particular call, did they do that by -- did they do that at the very moment that the call was being listened to or did they at a later time go back and listen to the tape and write out that conversation, since it was a potentially relevant conversation?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, they would listen to the tapes and transcribe them. But this could have been done simultaneously, too, although it would be very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I take it it might be possible to do it simultaneously in very short conversations, but for longer conversations the practice was to go back and transcribe the tape. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, once such a tape was -- once such a transcript was written out, the procedure was that it should be given to the -- whoever the supervisor was or the person coordinating the activities. Is that correct -- or coordinating their activities, I should say?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And then that supervisor then had to take a decision whether to forward it higher up the chain of information or pass it to other people or to act on it in a variety of different possible ways. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, in the case of the Minister of the Interior, it was not your job to look at every single of these transcripts that got brought into being. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As the Minister of the Interior, it was not my job to look at any of these transcripts. While I performed those duties, I did not read any of the transcripts that had been compiled by the operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, now there are some transcripts that even though I understand what you say about that, there's still some that I have to show you, but I still have some other preliminary questions before we get to that. Once the supervisor, whoever that was, had acted upon the information in an appropriate way and advised the appropriate people about that information, it then became necessary to file that transcript. And what I want to ask you is about the procedure of filing those transcripts. Firstly -- actually, I'll ask you firstly about the tapes. Firstly, the individual tapes upon which the telephone conversations were recorded were actually in very short supply in Bosnia during the war. Is that correct? In other words, there was actual physical shortage of such tapes to use?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no such information, according to which it wasn't possible to carry out certain tasks, as there were insufficient tapes. I never received such information. I believed that tapes were always available, and that was an obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I'll put the question slightly differently. Is it the fact that the tapes that were used on a day-by-day basis were at some stage in the proceedings transferred onto a large master tape or re-recorded on a large master tape?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one might say that that was the case. The tapes were used twice; tapes that had already been used were re-used. Tapes that were no longer important were re-used. If the people responsible for these matters believed that a certain tape was no longer important, that tape would then be re-used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Thank you. And then the master tape that I've referred to would then have to be archived. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no other tapes. There was the master tape. There was just one cassette tape or whatever you want to call it. It was always placed in the archives, and it was always related to the document that had been drafted by the individuals we have called operators. It wasn't possible to make tape recordings of other tapes. There was only one tape placed in the archives, unless an official request was made to proceed otherwise, but I'm not familiar with any such requests having been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, could you just tell us what's the official name of those archives? What was the official name of the archives in 1993 and what's the official name of those archives today?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is only one organisational unit within the SDB. It was the technical department; that is what we called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. So when speaking of the place where archives are kept, is it meaningful to speak of the archives of the SDB or should I use some other term?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was placed in the archives of the technical department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the same procedure applied to the filing of the transcript as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the procedure was a little different in that case. The transcripts were made available to those in charge of a certain case. An operator is in charge of a certain case, and this operator would provide written reports based on the tapes. But according to the protocol and certain protocol regulations, this was coded. The documents had a code so that they could be traced. The documents might be part of a file on a certain individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Thank you for that explanation. And finally, there was in place a legal and lawful way -- a legal and lawful procedure for the destruction of tapes and files. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a procedure for the destruction of all the documents that the service had, and this included these documents we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And that procedure was, if you like, controlled by a need to justify the destruction of any documents, if that had to be done, and to record such justification in writing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could say that that is correct, but I would like to add that there are certain criteria that have to be respected, certain documents have to be retained for a certain period of time, and then they are destroyed in accordance with the rules. A commission is established in order to make sure that everything is done in a regular manner. A record is compiled on the documents destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And the record of destroyed documents is, itself, preserved within those archives. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have to check the documents that regulate this field, but the record is then retained for a certain period of time. And then that document can also be destroyed after some time has elapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Now, there are some specifics of the account you've given already, which we're going to return to when we come to some concrete documents. But I now wish to turn to some concrete documents, and before I do so I just have some narrative questions to ask leading up to one document, the first that we're going to deal with. You indicated -- could I just indicate where the questions are going so that you follow the line of questioning. I'm now going to ask you some brief questions about the lead-up to Trebevic and then I'm going to come back to a document here, okay, so that's what coming so that you know. It's the fact that in the two weeks or so before -- sorry, Trebevic happened on the 26th of October of 1993, is that correct, Operation Trebevic was carried out?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably correct. It was a long time ago, but I know that it was at the end of October 1993. As I have seen in the documents and the plans, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we had evidence from General Karavelic that there was significant planning in the fortnight or so before the 26th of October, and I just wanted to ask you: Does that accord with your memory, that in those two weeks or possibly even more time before Trebevic you and also General Jasarevic and also the soldiers, Karavelic and others, were engaged in significant planning for Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle I would agree with that, but he did this as part of his duties. He performed certain acts to prepare for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I understand that each of you had a different function to perform in this plan. But is it also the fact that in that -- in that, let us say, two weeks or so before Trebevic you liaised closely with General Jasarevic and indeed other persons involved in Trebevic about the activities of the 9th and 10th Brigade and also to some degree about the activities of Sefer Halilovic. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true. I was not closely cooperating with Karavelic or with General Jasarevic, not during the preparation or after. Those were operative preparations, and then duties were carried out at the operative level. If I was involved in any preparations, as far as that was concerned, I must have talked to General Delic. As far as Nedzad Ugljanin and the chief of the SDB sector certainly cooperated far more closely with these officers that you have referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just ask that the witness be shown Defence document D -- this is 65 ter number D404. This is going to have to be circulated in hard copy, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 436.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I believe we have Bosnian copies for everyone in court because this document will be used to explain some of the notations as well, but I ask also that the English version be given to all those who are operating in English in this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Jas -- sorry, pardon me. Mr. Alispahic, I just explain what's coming here. This is a particular transcript which you may or may not have seen yourself; we're not presuming that you have. But whether you have or you haven't, I'll ask you some comment on some features about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You, Your Honours, it seems that the Defence copy of this statement has inadvertently gone missing. So I wonder if -- the one that's been placed on the ELMO, I wonder if I could have that for my own use. You, Your Honours, there's an issue that will have to be faced here concerning the date of this document. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, could I just ask you to take the opportunity to read that what time I raise a procedural matter with the Judge, and then I can ask you questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Bosnian version of this is longer than the -- than the English version. And the reason for that is that we've only translated the call that we're interested in, but it arises from a longer transcript and the date of that transcript can be discovered from the front page of the Bosnian. We'll ask the witness to explain all of that, but you don't have that in English. You just have the call in English. And because that arose after a number of other calls, you'll see at the front page of the Bosnian on the left-hand side the date is to be found of this call. On a previous occasion this has been referred to and we didn't have a date for it, and we've hopefully rectified that situation at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just ask, was this shown to Mr. Jasarevic or put to him when he testified?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think it was, Your Honours. Can I just -- can I just indicate there was a shortcoming when we showed it to General Jasarevic -- Your Honour, I've started attributing ranks today, I'm sorry, Mr. Jasarevic. And the transcript is at the 3rd of March, pages 77 to 78 where this was put to him, but at that time we didn't have the full Bosnian so we couldn't put a date to him properly. So we're going to try to rectify that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alispahic, the call I'm interesting in is really not the Ivan Brigic call, which is the first one, it's there, it's a call that's recorded there, but the one I'm interested in is the call to Jusuf Jasarevic on the following page. And I'm going to ask you some questions about that in a minute. But first I'm going to ask you some formal questions about the document and just get you to explain some of the markings on this document. Firstly could I ask that you explain the markings at the top left corner of the first page. So I'm now holding up the page to just indicate -- do you see the word "MUP" at the top left?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It says MUP, RBiH, and then SDB. Why are those letters written there? In formal terms, what's the purpose of them being there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are abbreviations. The Ministry of the Interior of the Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And why have they been put there -- in formal terms on this document, why were they written there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was usual practice. It was the usual heading put there by the operatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. The next line says "sector SDB Sarajevo." And that refers to the Sarajevo branch of the SDB. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And again, this is simply correct procedure on behalf of the operator to write that there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can we go to the next -- can you just confirm this. This document here, as you'll see, is dated 13/10/1993, and at that date was Mr. Mujezinovic the person who had the duty as commander of the sector of the SDB Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Pardon me. The interpreter didn't catch your answer on that occasion. Would you mind repeating it, please.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic was the chief of the Sarajevo SDB sector in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I must indicate to you, please feel to correct it if I use "commander" and it should be chief or director and it should be chief, please always fix that up because later we have to deal with this transcript. Very well. Thank you. Could you please go to the next line where the word, I think it is "objeljenje" 03 is to be found. Could you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's probably the code or the number that relates to the department where this sort of job is done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The department within the SDB. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Once again, that's just a proper notation -- a typical notation by the operator. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could we go to the next line, please. Could you just explain what is written there and what it means.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must say I can't be considered an expert as regards procedures used by the SDB. My testimony is to be understood in the following way, and I will do my best to provide whatever information, understanding I have of these procedures. I am a former chief of the MUP and SDB, but I never once found myself in a situation where I was expected to produce this sort of document myself, personally. I wish to make this abundantly clear and therefore not be asked any questions that might be asked of an expert. I might inadvertently make errors and this is something I wish to avoid. What's under consideration now is a purely technical matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we understand and we're grateful to you for that indication. I'm still going to ask you the questions, but we appreciate exactly what your position was. You were the minister; you weren't a technician. Now, having said that, what do you understand to be the meaning of that line, "radnik," and followed by the words 50143? Is that the worker's number?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be. There is a code and behind this code there should be a person and the person's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. The next line, what is the -- what do you understand that to mean, the one with "broje" or "brodje"?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume this is the numbering. It's a technical procedure. Numbers are used for tapes that are listened to. That is just my take on it; it need not be the case. It is an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And following that is the date given, 13/10/1993. Could you --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just to proceed, there's then some further information underneath that, and I just want to ask you this: Do you recall that -- you may not recall every detail of this document, but I'll ask you. When you signed the -- do you recall signing an approval or a decision for the implementation of operative measures against Sefer Halilovic back in June, at some time, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember signing this, but if I did the signature should be valid at the level of the Ministry of the Interior for this measure to be applied. There should be a document in the SDB archives authorising them to do whatever they were supposed to do and explaining how they should go about their work where members of the army were concerned. I really can't recall this document right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Look, I -- there is a document I want to show you. Could you -- could we keep that one alive, please, at the moment while I just show the other document. This is a document that's uploaded, so this is in the system. And could the witness please be shown Defence 65 ter number D157. Its number is DD00-0698. Now, there's a document that's going to come up -- up out of history, actually, you'll see -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be MFI 437.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before we go on, the transcript doesn't seem to indicate it, but the last document which was shown to the witness, MFI 436, is in fact a translation of MFI 234, which was shown to Mr. Jasarevic. I'm just saying that the two are actually linked together on the transcript and we know the documents are. I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: My friend is both right and wrong, Your Honour. What happened with that document as that because of the date issue we withdraw it and so it did start off with an MFI number, and we ended up -- because it was simply incapable of getting a date, we didn't press ahead with attempting to tender that. My friend is right, I think, but I think it will turn out there's another document that has now got that. That became an unoccupied MFI number. So we do ask for it to be given another MFI number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But for this Bench we'll only admit one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, but the other one is not -- doesn't exist anymore, so we'll need to give it a new number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, the current document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I also give the Prosecutors a copy of this -- the document is on the screen, but because it might need some flipping backwards and forwards we have just got a copy of it to give the Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sorry about that, Mr. Alispahic. Would you mind just looking at the screen now, please. And do you see there -- and I think probably -- I'm not sure how your Bosnian one is set out there. It's one page in Bosnian. Do you see -- would you mind just having a look at that and tell us if now after 11 years that can assist your memory about what happened.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that this is a state security service document. It was produced in 1993. The service imposed a measure against Mr. Halilovic. There was a proposal by the SDB chief. The proposal was approved, and I signed the decision to take these measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a perfectly valid document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. That was going to be my next question. There's no suggestion that it's a sneaky or sly document. What I want to put to you is what you just said, that is perfectly legitimate and valid and you followed all the right procedures in doing that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I understand that. Well, now, having regard, then, to the substance of the document, here there seems to be two measures proposed in the second line. There's "agava" and "zolja" operative measures. Now, at the moment I'm only concerned really with the "zolja" measures. The "zolja" measures, that was the telephone tapping, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I offer that document for tender, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D437.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks. Could we come back now to the other MFI document --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, that will be MFI 436.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes -- sorry, that's the -- 436 is the conversation, thank you, yes. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Pardon me, we're jumping but I'm grateful to you for your attention about that. Now, coming back to that here, is it the fact that the code name Skup you see two lines below -- you see there's a section in the middle here, I'm pointing to it, which you may be able to see on the transcript there. There's a reference to the name Skup, S-k-u-p. Now, that was the name attributed to Sefer Halilovic, wasn't it, in the course of this?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be 100 per cent certain about this, but it's certainly possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Now I want to turn to the actual discussion that occurs between Halilovic and Jusuf Jasarevic. Do you see here that Sefer spoke to Jusuf Jasarevic and that a certain conversation is transcribed in relation to that? All right. Now, just what I'm asking you to focus on here is: Do you see that there's a reference there to -- or to Sefer -- to Sefer Halilovic saying: "In any case, we'll be in touch." And then he says: "Q. Has that lad Dzankovic arrived from down there?" And Jasarevic says: "He has." And Sefer says: "Have you talked to him?" And Jasarevic says: "Yes, I have, and I've tasked him with writing it down." And Sefer then goes on to say: "Yes, he must. He must write everything down." Now, my first question about that is at the time that conversation took place were you made aware of that conversation yourself?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no way I could have known about this. I would like to ask you to please not ask me to comment on the control of these communications. I have never seen any of these documents. I would need to study them to give you an opinion. They're just outside my scope, outside the scope of what I knew. And I think it would make no sense for me to read transcripts that I've never seen before. I'm here to speak the truth and to tell the Court what I know, but it would be extremely cumbersome for me to go through all these transcripts I have never seen before and provide you with mere speculations as to what I believe is or is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Let me just assure you I would not ask you to speculate over the truth or otherwise of these documents, and that's not the reason I'm asking you those questions. What I'm asking you about you've answered, I think. You did -- you were not aware of this particular telephone call. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, no, it's just important to establish the fact of whether you did or didn't. And I take it what your answer is, you did not know about this telephone call. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I knew. I'm trying as hard as I can, but I can't remember that I ever memorised this conversation, that it ever took place. But it only seems natural that Jasarevic and General Halilovic communicated. That strikes me as perfectly natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I offer that document for tender now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's an outstanding similar document which we attempted to tender through Mr. Karavelic which is MFI 390, which on the face of it bears all the same indicia of reliability of a telephone conversation between Mr. Karavelic and Mr. Halilovic, as this one does between Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Jasarevic. There was a Defence objection to our tendering that. Now, clearly one can't go in without the other if they're in the same category of documents; that's our attitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I must say it sounds as if my friend is not objecting but that he says that it creates a strong argument in favour of the other one. There may be differences with the other one. He must be said to have a point, however. And of course I do press for -- I press for this one here. I think the -- 390 is pending. Perhaps that can be clarified. I don't think you've ruled on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So I think my learned friend gets another weight in the balance in that argument, if I may put it that way, but I do press for this one to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe this Bench has already made a decision that we'll admit all the intercept documents all together in the future. And the -- if you insist, we could admit this document. However, I have to remind you that you have to remember the Prosecution's position on this very issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: On document 390, I indicate to the Court I'm fully aware of the Prosecution's position. And as I say, that one's pending and Mr. Weiner and I had had some discussions about all of this. So perhaps when that comes to be ruled upon, it may be that we might have something else to say about it. Just right at the moment I'm just offering that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can I indicate, there are others but this one is in its own category for obvious reasons, so we offer it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Now we could say that this document is admitted into the evidence. And maybe sometime next week, since the Defence case is approaching -- since the Prosecution case is approaching to an end, we might find some time to discuss the admission of the evidence, especially for those intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I believe it's time for us to break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just have the liberty of asking one more question because I don't want to leave Mr. Alispahic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to clarify something about these documents generally. I take it from your answers what you say is you don't recall seeing any of these transcripts, because I've actually got quite a lot here, but you don't recall seeing any of them. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, this will assist the course of cross-examination tomorrow so I'm just going to ask you about it. Did you see any transcripts from the 26th of October itself, the day when Ramiz Delalic, Celo, was arrested? Did you see any transcripts of this nature relating to that day?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to have a look to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And final --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But please, do bear in mind that we need a clear chronology of these events and later when documents were processed and used and such-like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, okay. Thank you for those answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And Your Honours, we'll proceed tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I believe that the hearing for today is adjourned, and we'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 27th day of May, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
